setting.name: Bellweather
setting.summary: A small village of a square, a manor, an inn, a greenhouse, a church vestry and a doctor's surgery. Edmund Vale of Vale Manor is dead; the investigation begins the next morning.

rules.text: Getting between any two places in Bellweather takes at least the walking time along the lanes; nobody can be in two places at once.
When a person faces someone and strikes with the right hand, the blow lands on the victim's left side. A left-handed blow lands on the victim's right side.
A village constable who is first on the scene of a death covers the body with his own cape until the doctor arrives.

people.name: Clara Vale
people.voice: Composed and guarded; courteous but says little, quietly deflecting private matters. Speaks briefly.
people.public: Edmund’s younger sister. She manages the manor and has asked that its private affairs remain private.

people.name: Rowan Pike
people.voice: A plain-spoken working man; blunt and practical, short sentences, no flourishes.
people.public: The manor’s groundskeeper. His bandaged hand and green coat have become subjects of village conversation.

people.name: Silas Voss
people.voice: A precise, careful solicitor; measured and a touch formal, but concise — never rambling.
people.public: A precise, courteous solicitor who keeps an office in the vestry. He handled Edmund’s estate accounts.

people.name: Ada Finch
people.voice: A warm, chatty innkeeper; colloquial and quick to share impressions, though she runs on a little.
people.public: The Rook & Lantern’s proprietor. She knows everyone’s habits and is certain she saw something useful last night.

people.name: Dr Iris Marsh
people.voice: Measured and clinical; direct and concise, stays to what she observed.
people.public: Methodical and direct. She examined Edmund’s body and treated a patient at the greenhouse last night.

people.name: Arthur Bell
people.voice: A plain, gruff country constable; terse and matter-of-fact, everyday speech — never bureaucratic or long-winded.
people.public: Bell has secured the manor and asked you to investigate. He will hear an accusation when you can explain it with evidence.

people.name: Edmund Vale
people.public: Master of Vale Manor, found dead the morning the investigation begins.

objects.name: Half-burned letter
objects.desc: A letter in Edmund's hand, mostly burned in the study grate; a few lines about estate figures survive.

objects.name: Brass candlestick
objects.desc: A heavy candlestick from the study mantel, found on the hearthrug.

objects.name: Estate ledger
objects.desc: The account book of Vale Manor, kept by the estate solicitor.

objects.name: Constable's cape
objects.desc: A dark wool police cape with a numbered collar badge, left hanging in the inn taproom.

objects.name: Office day-book
objects.desc: Silas Voss's daily record of office work, kept open on his vestry desk.

objects.name: Post-mortem notes
objects.desc: Dr Marsh's written findings on Edmund Vale's body, prepared for the coroner.

objects.name: Drawing-room dust sheet
objects.desc: A linen dust sheet taken off the drawing-room sofa and spread over Edmund's body.

candidates.label: Clara Vale, his sister and heir

attitudes.content: The estate ledger does not reconcile; money has been diverted.
To confront Silas and put the matter before the county law society.
Ruin and prison if Edmund exposes the embezzlement.
To silence Edmund and destroy his letter before it is posted.
To keep ordinary office hours so that nothing seems amiss.
An evening away from the manor after quarrelling with Edmund.
To finish potting the late cuttings.
To attend any patient who sends for her.
To keep the inn running through the evening.
A pint after his rounds.
To go home to bed and settle things with Edmund in the morning.
That the village will learn he sat in the Rook through hours he should have spent walking the late beat.
That nobody gossip about her crying alone at the inn after the quarrel.
To keep her promise to Miss Vale and say nothing of her evening unless it is already known.
To make his office day-book show he was at his desk through the evening.
That the letter's line about her allowance will make her, the heir who quarrelled with Edmund, look guilty.
To keep her post-mortem findings for the coroner and release them only on the constable's authority.
To keep her writing case out of anyone's hands until she is sure she is not suspected.
A doctor should vouch only for what she observed; she did not look at a clock during the call.
To keep the night's door slate with her coroner's papers, since her own movements bear on the inquest.
Not to name a gentleman on a lamp-lit glimpse unless something solid shows she did not imagine it.
To keep everyone out of the manor and its garden until he trusts whoever is asking.
To spare Constable Bell the gossip of his cape being left in her taproom, and keep it out of sight until someone asks after it.
To cover the bare peg so no regular asks whose coat hung there all evening.
To cover Mr Vale decently at once, even though his cape is gone and he must use whatever the house has.

Rowan knew from Edmund's visit a fortnight before the murder that Edmund suspected Silas had been siphoning off church funds, disguised in the books as fees and copying work, amounting to nearly four hundred pounds from the Michaelmas accounts.

events.summary: Edmund writes a letter about the ledger discrepancies in his study.
Silas works in his vestry office.
Silas calls at the study; Edmund confronts him about the accounts.
Silas strikes Edmund with the brass candlestick.
Silas throws Edmund's letter into the grate and leaves before it fully burns.
Silas works on in his office, and its lamps burn late.
Clara dines alone in the inn's private parlour.
Clara returns to the manor and retires without disturbing Edmund's closed study.
Clara finds Edmund dead in his study at dawn.
Rowan pots cuttings in the greenhouse.
A pane gives way and cuts Rowan's left hand badly.
Iris sees evening patients at the surgery until sent for.
Iris stitches and bandages Rowan's hand in the greenhouse.
Rowan rests in his greenhouse quarters.
Iris returns to the surgery and writes up her notes.
Ada serves the taproom and parlour all evening.
Bell drinks in the taproom after his rounds.
Leaving the parlour, Clara quietly asks Ada to keep her evening to herself.
Bell hurries out of the taproom unseen and leaves his cape on the peg.
Silas writes timed day-book entries for 21:30 to 22:00, as if he had worked at his desk throughout.
Clara pulls the unburnt corner of Edmund's letter from the grate and hides it in her writing case.
Iris examines Edmund's body in the study and writes up her findings for the coroner.
Clara hurriedly wipes the soot off her fingers, misses her cuff, and locks her writing case, keeping it with her.
Leaving on the greenhouse call, Iris chalks where she has gone on the surgery door slate.
Back at the surgery, Iris chalks her return time under the earlier line.
Bell signs his beat card at the square pillar box at 20:55, then heads for the Rook.
Before leaving for the manor, Iris unhooks the unwiped door slate and files it with her coroner's papers.
Silas slips out of the garden door; his cane and shoes sink into the watered border under the terrace lamp.
Bell secures the manor and ropes off the garden door and terrace border.
At closing, Ada lifts Bell's cape off the taproom peg and hides it under her aprons in the scullery.
Ada hangs a dried hop bine over the bare peg by the settle, hiding the pale patch.
Bell stands his morning post in the square in tunic alone, cold and evasive about his missing cape.
With no cape, Bell drags a dust sheet off the drawing-room sofa and spreads it over Edmund's body.

signs.title: The doctor’s examination notes
signs.text: Examination of the deceased, Edmund Vale, reveals a single heavy blow to the back of the head, the skull fractured beneath the scalp wound. There is no evidence of any other injury or struggle, and the wound alone was sufficient to cause instant collapse. Death occurred between half past nine and ten o'clock, and I judge it to have been immediate, with no interval of lingering life.
signs.show: The examination notes show Edmund Vale died from a single heavy blow to the back of the head, likely between half past nine and ten that night. Does that fit with what you know?

reactions.silas: That window merely confirms I was at my desk, as my day-book shows. A single blow suggests a struggle got quickly out of hand — tragic, but it hardly points to me. I had no cause to wish Edmund harm.

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Marsh on the body
signs.text: He died at once, poor soul — a single heavy blow to the back of the head did the deed, and death came upon him right there between half past nine and ten o'clock, with no time for him to suffer long.
signs.ask: Doctor, what did you find when you examined Edmund?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says the fatal blow was struck by a blunt object with some force, sometime between half past nine and ten last night. Does that match what you saw?
signs.confront: You said he died from one heavy blow to the head, sometime between half past nine and ten. Is that your full assessment?

signs.speaker: bell
signs.title: Arthur Bell on the evening
signs.text: I did my rounds same as always, stopped in for a pint after, then went about my business. Nothing more to it than that.
signs.confront: You told me you did your rounds as usual, stopped for a pint, and went about your business. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he did his rounds as usual, stopped for a pint, then went about his business. Does that match what you know of his evening?

signs.speaker: iris
signs.title: Dr Iris Marsh on the evening
signs.text: I was seeing to patients at the surgery until I was called out to tend a hand injury, and I saw to that before returning to write up my notes. I did not mark the hour by any clock, only that I went and came back and got on with my work.
signs.confront: You said you were seeing patients, then called out to tend a hand injury, then returned to write up notes, without marking any times. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she was seeing patients at the surgery, then was called out to tend a hand injury before returning to write up her notes, though she marked no times. Does that fit with what you know?

signs.speaker: ada
signs.title: Ada Finch on the evening
signs.text: Oh, I was run off my feet all evening, love, taproom and parlour both - never had a moment to sit down. Can't say I noticed much else with all that going on, truth be told.
signs.confront: You told me you were run off your feet all evening and didn't notice much else. Is that really all you can tell me?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says she was run off her feet in the taproom and parlour all evening and noticed little else. Does that sound right to you?

signs.speaker: silas
signs.title: Silas Voss on the evening
signs.text: I was at my desk in the vestry office the whole evening, working through the accounts by lamplight, as my day-book will show. I kept to my usual hours and saw no one after I finished at the church.
signs.confront: You told me you were at your desk in the vestry office all evening and saw no one after church. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Voss says he was at his desk in the vestry office all evening working through the accounts, and saw no one after leaving the church. Does that match what you know?

signs.speaker: rowan
signs.title: Rowan Pike on the evening
signs.text: Was in the greenhouse, potting up the late cuttings. Cut my hand on a broken pane, got it bandaged, then stopped in my quarters there the rest of the night.
signs.confront: You said you were potting cuttings, cut your hand, had it bandaged, and stayed in your quarters the rest of the night. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Pike says he was in the greenhouse potting cuttings, cut his hand on a broken pane, had it bandaged, and stayed in his quarters the rest of the night. Does that fit with what you saw?

signs.speaker: clara
signs.title: Clara Vale on the evening
signs.text: I took a quiet supper alone in the parlour at the inn, then came straight home to the manor and went up to bed. I didn't look in on Edmund's study - I meant to sort things out with him this morning.
signs.confront: You told me you supped alone, came straight home, and went to bed without looking in on the study. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Miss Vale says she took a quiet supper alone at the inn, then came straight home to bed without looking in on Mr Vale's study. Does that match what you know?

signs.title: Dr Marsh on the greenhouse call
signs.text: "I left the surgery as soon as I was sent for and went straight to the greenhouse. I didn't look at a clock; I was busy. Mr Pike's left palm was laid open by glass. Eleven stitches. I stayed until he was steady, then walked straight back. He never left the bench the whole time I was there. He'd lost too much blood to go anywhere."
signs.speaker: iris
signs.reading: The door slate shows she went out at 21:05 and was back at 22:55. The walk each way takes ten minutes, so she was at the greenhouse with Pike from about 21:15 to 22:45. That covers the whole of the treatment, from 21:20 to 22:40.
signs.ask: Dr Marsh, what happened when you were called to the greenhouse?
signs.show: Dr Marsh says she went straight to the greenhouse, gave Mr Pike eleven stitches to his palm, and that he never left the bench while she was there. Would you say that's accurate?
signs.confront: Dr Marsh says she gave you eleven stitches in the greenhouse and that you never left the bench while she was there. Is that right?

reactions.rowan: Aye, that's right. Glass gave way while I was potting, cut me bad, and Dr Marsh saw to it right there. I didn't move off that bench till she was done with me.

concede.s_slate: Yes, alright - the slate has it plain: I was out at nine-oh-five and back by ten-fifty-five, and Pike hadn't the strength to stir the whole time. I said I didn't mind the clock because I wasn't watching it, not to hide anything, only because I was too busy stitching him to note the hour.

signs.direct: Dr Marsh says she stitched your hand eleven times in the greenhouse and that you never left the bench the whole time. Is that so?

signs.title: Constable Bell's evening
signs.text: "Right. That's mine. Signed my first point and walked straight into the Rook. Should've been walking the beat. Don't know the clock time. Stayed till twenty past eleven. Mrs Finch was behind that bar the whole time, never stepped out. Saw Miss Vale go through to the little parlour too."
signs.speaker: bell
signs.unlock: When you hand Bell the cape he left at the Rook, he knows you've found out where he spent the evening and stops dodging the question.
signs.reading: The beat card shows Bell signed at the square pillar box at 20:55. The square is three minutes' walk from the Rook, so he was in the taproom by 21:00. From then until 23:20 he could see Mrs Finch.
signs.ask: Constable Bell, how did you spend your evening?
signs.show: Constable Bell says he went straight into the Rook instead of walking his beat, and stayed until twenty past eleven, with Mrs Finch behind the bar the whole time. Does that match what you remember?
signs.confront: You told me you went straight into the Rook and stayed until twenty past eleven, with Mrs Finch never leaving the bar. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.ada: Oh, that's just as it was. I was behind the bar the whole evening, never stepped out, and I did see Miss Vale go through to the parlour. Constable Bell's a good lad, always in for a pint at his post.

concede.s_beatcard: Aye, the card shows I signed on at eight fifty-five, not nine, but it's the Rook I mean all the same - Mrs Finch never left that bar the whole time I was in there. I said I didn't know the clock because I wasn't minding it, not because I'd owt to hide.

signs.direct: Constable Bell says that on the night in question he went straight into the Rook and stayed till twenty past eleven, and that you were behind the bar the whole time without stepping out. Is that so?

signs.title: Mrs Finch on the parlour guest
signs.text: "Well, if the constable's said it... Miss Vale came in at nine, took the little parlour, had the soup and the chop and sat with her tea till gone eleven. I was in and out with the pot every quarter hour, so I'd know. She'd been crying, poor thing, and asked me not to say."
signs.speaker: ada
signs.unlock: Mrs Finch promised Miss Vale she'd keep quiet. Once you tell her the constable has already said Miss Vale was in the parlour, she thinks the promise no longer matters.
signs.ask: Mrs Finch, what can you tell me about your guest in the parlour?
signs.show: Mrs Finch says Miss Vale took the little parlour from nine until past eleven, had soup and a chop, and had been crying. Can you confirm that's what happened?
signs.confront: Mrs Finch says you sat in the little parlour from nine until past eleven, had soup and a chop, and had been crying. Is that so?

reactions.clara: That's true enough. I wanted an evening to myself, and Mrs Finch was kind not to press me on why. I'd rather not say more than that.

signs.direct: Mrs Finch says you sat in the little parlour from nine until gone eleven, had soup and a chop, and had been crying. Is that so?

signs.title: A cape from the scullery
signs.text: Mrs Finch goes into the scullery and brings out a dark wool police cape from under a pile of aprons. The collar badge is numbered. It smells of pipe smoke and beer, and something stiff is folded into the inside pocket.
signs.unlock: You show Mrs Finch the blue wool from the bare peg. She has no wish to lie about her own taproom, so she admits she put away what was left hanging there and fetches it from the scullery.
signs.show: This is a police cape found hidden under aprons in your scullery, with a numbered collar badge and something stiff tucked in the pocket - can you explain how it came to be here?

reactions.ada: Oh! That's Constable Bell's cape, sir, plain as day—badge number and all. I only tucked it away so the regulars wouldn't be nattering about whose coat that was, hanging there all evening. No harm meant by it, I'm sure.

signs.title: The vestry office day-book
signs.text: Mr Voss's day-book lies open on his desk. In his neat hand: '9.30 p.m. Hollins conveyance, fair copy begun. 9.45 Copy finished; rent summary posted. 10.00 Ledger, Michaelmas quarter, to close.' The entries above, for the afternoon, are just as tidy.

reactions.silas: That is my day-book, Inspector, kept as I always keep it — a fair copy, a rent summary posted, the ledger set to close. You will find every entry in my own hand, precise to the minute, exactly as my habit is.

signs.show: This is Mr Voss's day-book, with tidy entries timing his work right up to ten o'clock that night. Does that match what you know of his evening?
signs.direct: Your day-book shows neat entries timed between half past nine and ten o'clock. Were these really written as timed?

signs.title: Dr Marsh at the greenhouse door
signs.text: "His office? No. At about ten to ten I stepped out of the greenhouse door to empty the basin. Someone came out of the manor's garden door and passed under the terrace lamp. He wore a grey homburg and carried a silver-topped cane. That was Mr Voss. He crossed the border and made quickly for the lane. I took it for a late call on a client."
signs.speaker: iris
signs.unlock: Dr Marsh won't name a man on a lamp-lit glimpse. You tell her the day-book puts Mr Voss at his desk, then describe the cane holes and shoe prints in the border under that lamp. She's satisfied she didn't imagine him, and she says what she saw.
signs.ask: Dr Marsh, what did you see at the greenhouse door?
signs.confront: You told me you stepped out of the greenhouse door and saw a man in a grey homburg with a silver-topped cane cross the garden toward the lane, and took him for Mr Voss. Is that the whole of it?

reactions.silas: Dr Marsh is mistaken, or the light deceived her. I keep my homburg and cane by the office door for the walk home, nothing more sinister than a solicitor tired of his ledgers. My day-book will show I was at my desk the whole evening.

signs.show: Dr Marsh says that at ten to ten she saw Mr Voss come out of the manor's garden door in a grey homburg, carrying a silver-topped cane, and hurry for the lane. Is that true?

signs.title: A scorched corner of paper
signs.text: A corner of notepaper in Edmund's hand, browned at the edges: '...cannot let Voss's handling of the Michaelmas accounts pass. Near four hundred pounds unaccounted for... I shall put it before the county law society... Clara's allowance must wait until...' The rest is ash.
signs.unlock: Miss Vale hid the scrap because of the line about her allowance. Once Mrs Finch has vouched for her whole evening at the inn, she is no longer afraid of it and takes it out of her writing case.
signs.show: This is a scorched scrap of a letter in Edmund's hand, accusing Mr Voss of mishandling nearly four hundred pounds and threatening to report him to the law society - what can you tell me about it?

reactions.silas: I cannot speak to what Edmund chose to write or burn in his own grate. If he had concerns about the accounts, he never raised them with me in any formal way. I'd advise caution in reading too much into a scrap of ash.
reactions.clara: I... did not know that survived. Edmund and I quarrelled, yes, about money as much as anything—but I took nothing from that room, and I'll say no more of it.

signs.direct: I've read a scorched letter in Edmund's hand accusing you of mishandling nearly four hundred pounds from the Michaelmas accounts. Can you explain that?

signs.title: Dr Marsh's post-mortem notes
signs.text: 'Single depressed fracture to the right temple, above the ear. Blow delivered from in front and slightly above. Flecks of brass in the wound. No other injuries. No sign that the deceased turned away.'
signs.unlock: Dr Marsh keeps her findings for the coroner and releases them only on the constable's say-so. Once Bell stops dodging and is cooperating, he authorises it and she hands over the notes.
signs.reading: The blow came from in front and landed on Edmund's right temple. By the rule of how a facing blow falls, it was struck left-handed.
signs.show: The post-mortem notes describe a single blow to the right temple from in front, with flecks of brass in the wound - can you help me understand what struck him?

reactions.iris: The wound is consistent with what I observed: a single blow, from in front, above the ear. The brass flecks are notable—I'd want them matched against anything found at the scene. I have nothing further to add beyond what's written.
reactions.silas: That is a matter for the coroner and Dr Marsh's expertise, not for me to interpret. I was nowhere near Edmund that evening, as my day-book shows. I can offer no theory as to the weapon.

signs.title: Miss Vale and her writing case
signs.text: Miss Vale receives you in the morning room with a small leather writing case held on her lap, and she keeps a hand on it the whole time. There is a grey smear of ash on her right cuff. When the study grate comes up, she looks away and asks whether you would like tea.
signs.show: Miss Vale kept a writing case in her lap and her hand on it throughout, with ash on her cuff, and looked away when the study fire came up. Have you noticed her behaving this way?
signs.confront: You've kept your hand on that writing case the whole time we've spoken, and there's ash on your cuff. Why did you look away when I mentioned the study grate?

reactions.clara: It's simply my writing case—I keep it close from habit, nothing more. As for the grate, I'd rather not dwell on it. Shall I ring for tea?

signs.direct: You kept your writing case close the whole time we spoke, and there's ash on your cuff. You looked away when I mentioned the study grate. Is there something you'd like to tell me?

signs.title: The surgery door slate
signs.text: The small blackboard from the surgery door, now lying among Dr Marsh's coroner's papers. The chalk has not been wiped. In a brisk hand: 'Out: Vale greenhouse, 9.05 p.m.' Beneath it, in the same chalk: 'Returned 10.55. I.M.'
signs.unlock: Dr Marsh has put the slate with her papers for the coroner and gives them out only on the constable's authority. Once Bell is cooperating, he authorises it and she hands the slate over.
signs.show: This slate from your surgery door records Mr Pike going out to the greenhouse at 9.05 and your own return at 10.55 - can you confirm these times?

reactions.iris: Yes, that's my own hand and my own chalk—I went out to the greenhouse when Rowan sent for me, and returned when I'd finished. I didn't check a clock, but the slate was accurate as I wrote it.

signs.direct: Your surgery slate records you out to the greenhouse at 9.05 and back at 10.55. Is that accurate?

signs.title: A beat card in the cape pocket
signs.text: A folded police beat card from the cape's inside pocket, dated last night. 'Square, pillar box: 8.55 p.m. A.B.' is initialled in pencil. The later points, 'Greenhouse lane 10.30' and 'Church gate 11.30', have been left blank.
signs.unlock: The card is folded in the inside pocket of the cape; you find it when you take the cape down.
signs.show: This beat card from the cape shows you signed the square point at 8.55, but the greenhouse lane and church gate points were never marked - can you account for that?

reactions.bell: Aye, that's mine. Signed the pillar box right enough at 8.55. Rest of the round I... never mind that now — there's a dead man to see to.

signs.direct: Your beat card shows you signed the square at 8.55, but the later points for the greenhouse lane and church gate are blank. Why weren't they marked?

signs.title: The border by the garden door
signs.text: The border below the terrace lamp was watered at dusk and is still soft. It holds a line of narrow heel prints from a town shoe, heading for the lane gate. Beside them, at every second step, is a small round hole ringed by a crisp metal rim.
signs.unlock: Bell has roped off the garden door. Once he has stopped dodging and is cooperating, he lifts the rope and lets you look at the terrace border.
signs.show: The soft border below the terrace lamp shows narrow heel prints from a town shoe heading to the lane gate, with a small round hole beside them at every second step - do you know what made these?

reactions.silas: Heel prints in a wet border prove little; half the parish wears town shoes. I cannot account for every mark left near that lamp, nor would I try to invent an explanation to satisfy you.

signs.title: The peg behind the hops
signs.text: A dried hop bine hangs on the wall by the settle. When you lift it, you find a wooden peg with nothing on it. Around the peg the wall is yellow with pipe smoke, except for a long, narrow pale patch that hangs down from it. A few fibres of dark blue wool are caught on a splinter under the peg's head.
signs.unlock: Bell has plainly lost his cape and won't say where. Since the Rook is where a man sheds a coat, you search the taproom pegs and lift the hop bine that hangs over the one by the settle.
signs.show: Behind this hop bine there's an empty peg with a pale patch on the wall and a few dark blue wool fibres caught on a splinter beneath it - can you tell me what usually hangs there?

reactions.ada: Oh, that old peg! I hung the hops there myself, just to brighten the wall a bit—didn't care for that bare patch staring out at everyone. As for blue wool, well, all sorts hang their coats there of an evening, I couldn't tell you whose is whose.

signs.title: The constable in the morning chill
signs.text: Constable Bell stands by the pillar box in his tunic alone, though there is frost on the grass. He keeps rubbing his upper arms. When you remark on the cold, he says he's warm enough and turns the talk back to the manor.
signs.unlock: The sheet in the study means the constable came to the manor without his cape. So you go and find him at his post in the square and watch how he is standing up to the frost, rather than taking his word that he's warm enough.
signs.show: Constable Bell was standing by the pillar box in just his tunic despite the frost, rubbing his arms, and turned the talk from the cold back to the manor. Have you noticed him acting strangely like this?
signs.confront: You're stood out here in just your tunic despite the frost, rubbing your arms, and you brushed off my remark on the cold. Why is that?

reactions.bell: I'm warm enough, I told you. Never mind my arms, you want to be looking at that garden door, not fussing over my cape.

signs.direct: You're standing out here in just your tunic with frost on the grass, rubbing your arms against the cold, yet you insist you're warm enough and steer me back to talk of the manor. Why is that?

signs.title: The covering in the study
signs.text: Edmund Vale lies on the study floor under a linen dust sheet. It is creased from the drawing-room sofa and has a sofa-shaped grey outline of dust on it. Fluff trails across the hall from the drawing-room door. Nothing else has been laid over him.
signs.reading: The constable was the first official at the scene, and he would normally have covered the body with his own cape. Since a sofa sheet had to be used instead, he did not have his cape with him at dawn.
signs.show: The sheet over Mr Vale is creased as though taken from the drawing-room sofa, with dust marks and fluff trailing from that door - do you know who covered him and why?

reactions.bell: Aye, that's off the drawing-room sofa. Had no cape on me, so I used what was to hand — man deserved covering decent, not left bare on the floor.

signs.title: Rowan Pike on the vestry accounts
signs.text: Mr Edmund come by here a fortnight back, asking had I seen any timber sold off the estate. Said Voss had been putting church funds to his own use for months, dressing it up in the books as fees and copying work. Reckoned it was close on four hundred pound gone missing from the Michaelmas accounts.
signs.unlock: once you have a scorched corner of paper, you know what to ask
signs.speaker: rowan
signs.ask: Did Edmund ever say what he suspected Silas of doing with the money?
signs.confront: You told Rowan Pike that Voss had been dressing up church funds as fees and copying work, with close on four hundred pounds missing from the Michaelmas accounts. Is that the whole of it?
signs.show: Mr Pike says Edmund came to him a fortnight ago asking about estate timber and claiming Mr Voss had been siphoning off close to four hundred pounds from church funds. Do you know if that's true?

title: The Half-Burned Letter
synopsis: Edmund Vale was found dead in his study at Vale Manor.

clara: I manage Edmund's household at the manor, keeping the accounts of the kitchen and staff and seeing to the day-to-day running of the place.
Edmund was my elder brother and I have lived at the manor with him for years.
I know Silas as the family solicitor who has long handled our estate accounts, and I know Ada, Iris, Rowan and Bell as everyone in the village does.
rowan: I live and keep my tools in the greenhouse, where I spend most of my working hours.
I know Miss Clara and Mr Edmund as my employers, and I know Silas, Ada, Iris and Bell from the ordinary business of the village.
My bandaged hand and green coat are common knowledge in the village, as people have remarked on them.
silas: I handled Edmund's estate accounts and met with him from time to time on business.
I keep a day-book on my desk in the vestry to record my hours and the matters I attend to.
I know Clara through the Vale estate business, and I know Ada, Iris, Rowan and Bell as everyone in the village does.
ada: I keep the Rook & Lantern, the village inn, pouring drinks and keeping rooms for travelers.
I know most everyone in the village by their habits, since they pass through my taproom regularly.
I know Bell as a regular who stops in after his rounds, and I know Clara, Silas, Rowan and Iris as neighbours in the village.
I live at the inn and keep my accounts and keys to the cellar and rooms there.
iris: I know Clara, Silas, Ada, Rowan and Bell as patients and neighbours across the village.
bell: I live and keep my post in the square, and I answer to matters of village security.
I know Clara, Silas, Ada, Rowan and Iris as residents I look after in my rounds.

moods.silas: Composed and businesslike, going about his usual duties with nothing untoward showing.
moods.ada: Brisk and tight-lipped behind the bar, steering talk away from last evening and quietly tidying the taproom before anyone asks questions.
moods.iris: Calm but careful; tired from the call-out, keeping her notes close and choosing her words carefully about who she did or didn't see.
